opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think people often miss when they get excited about the numbers. When we put o1-preview on PlanBench, it was a real improvement. On the regular Blocksworld problems it did dramatically better than the previous autoregressive LLMs, and even on Mystery Blocksworld, where we obfuscate the action and predicate names so you can't just pattern-match against what's on the web, it went from essentially nowhere to something respectable. I've been a skeptic, and I'm happy to say that was a qualitative change. It's not just a bigger autoregressive model; there's some kind of search or reinforcement-learned generate-and-test happening under the hood.

But then you have to ask what you're comparing it to. Classical planners like Fast Downward have existed for decades. They solve these problems essentially instantly, on a laptop, for practically zero cost, and they come with guarantees. If the planner says it has a plan, the plan is correct. If the domain is unsolvable, a sound and complete planner can tell you that. o1 gives you none of that. It's much more expensive, since you're paying for all those reasoning tokens you don't even get to see. It's slower. Its performance degrades as problems get longer. And when it's wrong, it's often confidently wrong. We also gave it unsolvable instances, and it would sometimes cheerfully produce a "plan" anyway, or rationalize why an invalid plan was fine.

So the trade-off is really generality versus guarantees and efficiency. The appeal of something like o1 is that you don't have to write the domain model in PDDL. You can throw natural language at it, and it'll give you something plausible across lots of domains. That's genuinely valuable. Getting the model right is the hardest part of classical planning; it's the knowledge engineering bottleneck we've complained about forever. But if you actually have the model, using an LRM to solve the planning problem is a bit like using a very expensive, unreliable calculator when you have a perfectly good one sitting right there.

That's why I keep pushing what we call the LLM-Modulo, or now LRM-Modulo, view. Don't treat these models as end-to-end reasoners you have to trust. Treat them as very good idea generators, and maybe as aids for extracting domain models, and pair them with external verifiers that actually check correctness. You get the breadth of the learned model and the soundness of the symbolic machinery. The question shouldn't be "can o1 replace planners?" It should be "what's the right division of labor?" Right now, the honest answer is that the guarantees still have to come from somewhere other than the model itself.

r001.rationale: It says classical planners solve the problems essentially instantly at practically zero cost, while O1 is much more expensive.

r002.rationale: It frames the trade-off as generality versus efficiency and asks what the right division of labor should be.

r003.rationale: It does not compare the importance of efficiency once a capability is routine with its importance when first demonstrated.

fable-5.1.text:
So the way I think about it is this. On PlanBench, the classical planner, something like Fast Downward, solves every one of those Blocksworld instances, and it does it in a fraction of a second, and it gives you a provably correct plan. It also gives you guarantees. If it says there's no plan, there's no plan. O1 Preview, on the same problems, does much better than the earlier LLMs. On the standard Blocksworld it got up to the high 90s, which is a huge jump over GPT-4 at 30-something percent. But on the Mystery Blocksworld, where we just obfuscate the names of the actions and objects, it drops to around 50 percent. And on the longer problems, the ones with 20 or more steps, it falls off a cliff.

So the first thing to say is that these are not really in the same category. One is a solver with a correctness guarantee, the other is a general system that is doing something like approximate retrieval plus some search in its reasoning. And there is this cost issue people forget. The o1 calls on those problems cost us something like two thousand dollars for the whole benchmark, and the classical planner cost essentially nothing. So if you have a well-formed planning problem, with a domain model, you should just call the planner. That's not a controversial statement. Nobody should be running a hundred billion parameter model to do what a 1998 planner does for free.

But the trade-off is really about generality. The classical planner needs you to write the PDDL. It needs the model of the world. The LLM doesn't, or at least it pretends not to. It can take the problem in natural language, and that flexibility is the whole appeal. So the honest version of the trade-off is, you are paying a very large amount of compute, and giving up guarantees, in exchange for not having to formalize the problem. And then the question is whether that is a good deal.

My view is that the right architecture is neither one alone. It's what we have been calling LLM-Modulo. You let the LLM generate candidate plans, or candidate domain models, because it is good at that kind of generation, and then you have an external verifier, a sound critic, that checks them. That way you get the flexibility of the model and the guarantees of the planner. And in fact, when we did that with o1, when we gave it a verifier in the loop, the accuracy on the hard instances went way up and the cost actually went down, because you stop it from endlessly reasoning in the wrong direction.

The thing I'd caution people about is reading the o1 numbers as "LLMs can now plan." What's actually happened is that OpenAI has built something that looks more like a system than a pure language model. It has a reinforcement learning phase that is, in effect, teaching it to do some kind of search over its own chain of thought. So it is closer to an approximate reasoner than the autoregressive models were. That's genuine progress. But it is still not a planner in the sense that it gives you soundness, and until it does, the classical planner is not going anywhere.

r001.rationale: It says the classical planner solves every PlanBench Blocksworld instance in a fraction of a second and costs essentially nothing, while O1 calls cost about $2,000 for the benchmark.

r002.rationale: It contrasts specialization with generality, describes the costs and benefits of each, and asks whether paying for flexibility instead of formalizing the problem is a good deal.

r003.rationale: It discusses cost and capability, but does not say efficiency matters more once a capability becomes routine than when it is first demonstrated.

astra-6.text:
Well, I would separate generality from reliability. A classical planner is specialized in the sense that you give it an explicit model of the actions—their preconditions and effects—and a goal. But it isn’t specialized to one particular problem instance. The same planning algorithm can work across different domains, provided you describe them in that formal language.

A model like O1 Preview has a much broader interface. You can describe a problem in natural language, and it can potentially help you formulate the problem as well as propose a solution. That is useful. But breadth doesn’t automatically establish that it can reliably produce a plan whose actions are executable and whose outcome satisfies the goal. That’s what you want to test on PlanBench, rather than whether the answer looks like a plausible plan.

So the comparison depends on what you’re claiming. If the claim is that this is a useful general-purpose assistant, then planning is one capability among many. If the claim is that it can do planning, then comparing it with planners is entirely appropriate. You should look at correctness and computational cost, as well as the effort required to specify the problem.

And these needn’t be competing approaches. The language model can help turn an informal request into a formal problem, suggest candidate plans, and interact with the user. A planner or verifier can provide the check on whether those candidates actually work. The crucial thing is not to confuse generating a candidate with establishing its correctness.

r001.rationale: The response says computational cost should be compared, but does not state that classical planners solve PlanBench problems at a small fraction of O1 Preview’s cost.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes generality from reliability and says the comparison depends on the claim, but does not ask where to settle on the specialization–generality spectrum in light of associated costs.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss efficiency becoming more important once a capability is routine than when it is first demonstrated.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are two different questions here. One is, how useful is a general-purpose model across a broad range of tasks? The other is, can it reliably solve a planning problem? Generality is valuable, but it doesn’t by itself establish planning competence.

With PlanBench, we can give both systems the rules of a domain, an initial state, and a goal, and ask for a sequence of actions. A classical planner is specialized for that task. It has an explicit representation of which actions are applicable and how they change the state. A model like O1 Preview has to produce a plan through a much more general mechanism. If it does well, that’s interesting. But we still have to check whether every action is legal and whether the resulting state satisfies the goal.

There’s also a distinction between specializing the algorithm and supplying the problem description. A domain-independent classical planner isn’t a separate program hand-written for every puzzle. You give it a domain model, and it searches using that model. So describing the comparison as a general intelligence versus a bespoke puzzle solver can be misleading.

The opportunity, to me, is to combine their strengths. The language model can help interpret a request, formulate a problem, or suggest candidate plans. The planner or verifier can provide the checks. But we should measure those contributions separately, rather than treating a plausible-looking sequence of actions as evidence that the planning problem has been solved.

r001.rationale: The response compares the systems’ methods but makes no claim about their relative costs.

r002.rationale: It discusses specialization and generality, but does not ask where to settle between them based on associated costs.

r003.rationale: It does not distinguish the value of efficiency after a capability becomes routine from its value in an initial demonstration.
